<div class="page-shell">

<header class="masthead">
  <div class="eyebrow">WebR practical</div>
  <h1>Odds, log-odds, and odds ratios</h1>
  <p>In the last two lessons you fit a logistic regression of weak grip on age and learned that its coefficient is a change in log-odds. This practical takes the full chain into R: compute odds, take their log, fit the model, exponentiate the coefficients with <code>broom::tidy()</code>, and read the odds ratios the way they appear in papers.</p>
</header>

<section class="panel">

<h2>Overview</h2>

Logistic regression moves between four related quantities:

<ul class="tight-list">
  <li><strong>Probability</strong>: the share of people with the event. Between 0 and 1.</li>
  <li><strong>Odds</strong>: how often the event happens divided by how often it does not. <code>p / (1 - p)</code>.</li>
  <li><strong>Log-odds</strong>: the natural log of the odds. The scale the model fits its straight line on.</li>
  <li><strong>Odds ratio (OR)</strong>: the odds in one group divided by the odds in another. The number you report.</li>
</ul>

The odds ratio is the most important one for your day-to-day work, because it is how logistic regression results are reported in papers and how you will report them from R.

After answering the questions, your completion code will be revealed.

</section>

<section class="panel">

<h2>Part 1. From counts to odds</h2>

Odds compare the two sides of an event directly: how often it happens against how often it does not. Imagine a drug trial group of 10 patients in which 8 were cured and 2 were not.

</section>

<div class="webr-wrap">

<h3>R code: compute odds from counts</h3>

Run the cell. The first calculation uses counts. The second gets the same answer from the probability, using `p / (1 - p)`.

```{webr-r}
cured <- 8
not_cured <- 2

# odds from counts
cured / not_cured

# the same odds from the probability
p <- cured / (cured + not_cured)
p / (1 - p)
```

</div>

<div class="practice" data-answer="b">
  <div class="practice-title">Question 1</div>
  <p>The odds of being cured in this group are <strong>4</strong>. What does that mean?</p>
  <div class="choice-set">
<label><input type="radio" name="p0" value="a">The probability of being cured is 4.</label>
<label><input type="radio" name="p0" value="b">Being cured happened 4 times as often as not being cured.</label>
<label><input type="radio" name="p0" value="c">4 patients were cured.</label>
  </div>
  <button type="button">Check</button>
  <div class="practice-feedback" data-correct="Correct. Odds = cured / not cured = 8 / 2 = 4. The event happened 4 times as often as it did not. A probability can never be 4: probabilities stop at 1." data-incorrect="Not quite. Odds compare the two sides: 8 cured against 2 not cured, which is 4 to 1. A probability can never be 4."></div>
</div>

<div class="practice" data-answer="c">
  <div class="practice-title">Question 2</div>
  <p>In another group the odds of being cured are <strong>0.25</strong>. What does that tell you?</p>
  <div class="choice-set">
<label><input type="radio" name="p1" value="a">Being cured is more likely than not.</label>
<label><input type="radio" name="p1" value="b">The odds are impossible: odds cannot be below 1.</label>
<label><input type="radio" name="p1" value="c">Being cured is less likely than not: it happens 4 times less often than not.</label>
  </div>

  <div class="practice-feedback" data-correct="Correct. Odds below 1 mean the event is less common than its opposite. Flipping it: 1 / 0.25 = 4, so not being cured is 4 times as common." data-incorrect="Not quite. Odds below 1 are fine (they stop only at 0), and they mean the event is less likely than not. 1 / 0.25 = 4, so the opposite is 4 times as common."></div>
</div>

<section class="panel">

<h2>Part 2. Log-odds</h2>

Odds live on an unbalanced scale: they can grow without limit above 1, but they are squeezed between 0 and 1 below it. Taking the natural log fixes this. The log of 1 is 0, odds above 1 get a positive log, and odds below 1 get a negative log. This log of the odds, the <strong>log-odds</strong>, is the scale logistic regression fits its straight line on.

</section>

<div class="webr-wrap">

<h3>R code: take the log of some odds</h3>

Before running, predict the sign of each result: positive, zero, or negative. Then run.

```{webr-r}
log(4)      # odds above 1
log(1)      # odds exactly 1 (a 50-50 chance)
log(0.25)   # odds below 1

# shortcut: qlogis() goes straight from probability to log-odds
qlogis(0.8)
log(0.8 / 0.2)
```

</div>

<div class="practice" data-answer="a">
  <div class="practice-title">Question 3</div>
  <p>An event has probability <strong>0.5</strong>. What is its log-odds?</p>
  <div class="choice-set">
<label><input type="radio" name="p2" value="a"><code>0</code>, because the odds are 1 and <code>log(1) = 0</code>.</label>
<label><input type="radio" name="p2" value="b"><code>0.5</code>, the same as the probability.</label>
<label><input type="radio" name="p2" value="c"><code>1</code>, because the two sides are equal.</label>
  </div>
  <button type="button">Check</button>
  <div class="practice-feedback" data-correct="Correct. At p = 0.5 the odds are 0.5 / 0.5 = 1, and log(1) = 0. The log-odds scale is balanced around 0, which is the 50-50 point." data-incorrect="Not quite. At p = 0.5 the odds are 0.5 / 0.5 = 1, and the log of 1 is 0."></div>
</div>

<section class="panel">

<h2>Part 3. The model from the lessons</h2>

Time to refit the model you saw in the videos: KLoSA data on South Korean men aged 45 and above, modelling the probability of <strong>weak grip</strong> from <strong>age</strong>.

<ul class="tight-list">
  <li><strong>Outcome:</strong> <code>weak_grip</code> (1 = weak grip strength, 0 = normal)</li>
  <li><strong>Predictor:</strong> <code>age</code> (years)</li>
</ul>

Run the cell to read the data from GitHub and fit the model. `broom::tidy()` shows the coefficient table.

</section>

<div class="webr-wrap">

<h3>R code: fit the logistic regression</h3>

```{webr-r}
library(dplyr)
library(broom)

klosa <- read.csv("https://raw.githubusercontent.com/the-graph-courses/rsr_resources/main/data/28_klosa_men_grip.csv")

mod <- glm(weak_grip ~ age, family = binomial, data = klosa)

tidy(mod)
```

</div>

<details class="answer">
<summary>What you should see</summary>

Rounded, the coefficient table is:

```
term        estimate std.error statistic   p.value
(Intercept)   -8.82    0.319       -27.6  3.6e-168
age            0.117   0.00475      24.6  2.5e-133
```

The fitted line, on the log-odds scale, is the one from the lessons: log-odds of weak grip = -8.82 + 0.117 &times; age.

</details>

<div class="practice" data-answer="b">
  <div class="practice-title">Question 4</div>
  <p>In this output, the <code>estimate</code> for age is <strong>0.117</strong>. What does it mean?</p>
  <div class="choice-set">
<label><input type="radio" name="p3" value="a">Each extra year of age adds 0.117 to the probability of weak grip.</label>
<label><input type="radio" name="p3" value="b">Each extra year of age adds 0.117 to the log-odds of weak grip.</label>
<label><input type="radio" name="p3" value="c">Each extra year of age multiplies the odds of weak grip by 0.117.</label>
  </div>
  <button type="button">Check</button>
  <div class="practice-feedback" data-correct="Correct. Plain tidy() output is on the log-odds scale, so the coefficient is an additive change in log-odds per year of age." data-incorrect="Not quite. Without exponentiate = TRUE, the estimate column is on the log-odds scale: each year adds 0.117 to the log-odds."></div>
</div>

<section class="panel">

<h2>Part 4. Odds ratios with <code>exponentiate = TRUE</code></h2>

Log-odds are hard to explain to a reader, so papers almost never report them. Instead they report <strong>odds ratios</strong>. A difference in log-odds becomes a ratio of odds when you exponentiate (raise <em>e</em> to that power).

`broom::tidy()` does this for you: set `exponentiate = TRUE`, and add `conf.int = TRUE` so you also get the 95% confidence interval that papers expect.

</section>

<div class="webr-wrap">

<h3>R code: fill in the blank</h3>

Replace `____` with `TRUE` and run.

```{webr-r}
tidy(mod, exponentiate = ____, conf.int = TRUE)
```

</div>

<details class="answer">
<summary>Show the answer</summary>

```r
tidy(mod, exponentiate = TRUE, conf.int = TRUE)
```

Rounded, you should see:

```
term        estimate std.error statistic   p.value  conf.low conf.high
(Intercept) 0.000147   0.319       -27.6  3.6e-168  0.0000779 0.000272
age         1.124      0.00475      24.6  2.5e-133  1.114     1.135
```

The `estimate` column is now an odds ratio. For age it is 1.124, with 95% CI 1.114 to 1.135.

</details>

<div class="webr-wrap">

<h3>R code: check that this is just e to the power of the coefficient</h3>

```{webr-r}
coef(mod)["age"]        # the log-odds slope
exp(coef(mod)["age"])   # e^0.1168 = the odds ratio
```

</div>

<div class="practice" data-answer="c">
  <div class="practice-title">Question 5</div>
  <p>After exponentiating, the estimate for age is <strong>1.124</strong>. What does it mean?</p>
  <div class="choice-set">
<label><input type="radio" name="p4" value="a">The probability of weak grip rises by 1.124 each year.</label>
<label><input type="radio" name="p4" value="b">Men with weak grip are on average 1.124 years older.</label>
<label><input type="radio" name="p4" value="c">Each extra year of age multiplies the odds of weak grip by 1.124, about 12% higher odds per year.</label>
  </div>
  <button type="button">Check</button>
  <div class="practice-feedback" data-correct="Correct. An OR of 1.124 per year means the odds are multiplied by 1.124 for each additional year: 12.4% higher odds per year of age." data-incorrect="Not quite. The exponentiated coefficient is an odds ratio per one-unit change in the predictor: each year multiplies the odds by 1.124."></div>
</div>

<section class="panel">

<h2>Turning odds ratios into words</h2>

Papers state odds ratios in plain words. The rule: above 1, the percent <strong>higher</strong> is the OR minus 1. Below 1, the percent <strong>lower</strong> is 1 minus the OR.

<table class="or-table">
  <caption>Common odds ratios and how papers phrase them</caption>
  <thead>
    <tr><th>Odds ratio</th><th>In words</th></tr>
  </thead>
  <tbody>
    <tr><td><code>4.0</code></td><td>4 times the odds</td></tr>
    <tr><td><code>2.0</code></td><td>twice the odds (100% higher odds)</td></tr>
    <tr><td><code>1.5</code></td><td>50% higher odds</td></tr>
    <tr><td><code>1.12</code></td><td>12% higher odds</td></tr>
    <tr class="refrow"><td><code>1.0</code></td><td>no difference</td></tr>
    <tr><td><code>0.8</code></td><td>20% lower odds</td></tr>
    <tr><td><code>0.5</code></td><td>half the odds (50% lower odds)</td></tr>
    <tr><td><code>0.25</code></td><td>75% lower odds</td></tr>
  </tbody>
</table>

</section>

<div class="practice" data-answer="a">
  <div class="practice-title">Question 6</div>
  <p>A model of exercise and weak grip gives an odds ratio of <strong>0.8</strong> for regular exercisers. Which wording is right?</p>
  <div class="choice-set">
<label><input type="radio" name="p5" value="a">Regular exercisers had 20% lower odds of weak grip.</label>
<label><input type="radio" name="p5" value="b">Regular exercisers had 80% lower odds of weak grip.</label>
<label><input type="radio" name="p5" value="c">Regular exercisers had 0.8% lower odds of weak grip.</label>
  </div>
  <button type="button">Check</button>
  <div class="practice-feedback" data-correct="Correct. Below 1, percent lower = 1 minus the OR = 1 - 0.8 = 0.20, so 20% lower odds." data-incorrect="Not quite. Below 1, percent lower = 1 minus the OR. Here 1 - 0.8 = 0.20, so 20% lower odds."></div>
</div>

<section class="panel">

<h2>Part 5. Comparing groups</h2>

Predictors are often categories instead of numbers. Cut age into three groups: 45&ndash;64, 65&ndash;74, and 75+. R uses the first level (45&ndash;64) as the <strong>reference</strong>, and every odds ratio in the output compares one group with that reference.

</section>

<div class="webr-wrap">

<h3>R code: a categorical predictor</h3>

```{webr-r}
klosa <- klosa %>%
  mutate(age_group = cut(age,
                         breaks = c(44, 64, 74, Inf),
                         labels = c("45-64", "65-74", "75+")))

mod3 <- glm(weak_grip ~ age_group, family = binomial, data = klosa)

tidy(mod3, exponentiate = TRUE, conf.int = TRUE)
```

</div>

<details class="answer">
<summary>What you should see</summary>

Rounded:

```
term           estimate std.error statistic   p.value conf.low conf.high
(Intercept)      0.0958   0.0693      -33.8  8.1e-251   0.0834     0.110
age_group65-74   5.22     0.0936       17.7  8.8e-70    4.35       6.28
age_group75+    14.4      0.119        22.5  8.1e-112  11.5       18.3
```

There is no `age_group45-64` row. That group is the reference: the other two rows compare against it.

</details>

<div class="practice" data-answer="b">
  <div class="practice-title">Question 7</div>
  <p>The odds ratio for <code>age_group65-74</code> is <strong>5.22</strong>. What does it compare?</p>
  <div class="choice-set">
<label><input type="radio" name="p6" value="a">Men aged 65&ndash;74 with men aged 75+.</label>
<label><input type="radio" name="p6" value="b">Men aged 65&ndash;74 with the reference group, men aged 45&ndash;64.</label>
<label><input type="radio" name="p6" value="c">Men aged 65&ndash;74 with all other men combined.</label>
  </div>
  <button type="button">Check</button>
  <div class="practice-feedback" data-correct="Correct. Every OR from a categorical predictor compares one level with the reference level. Men aged 65-74 have 5.22 times the odds of weak grip compared with men aged 45-64." data-incorrect="Not quite. R compares each level with the reference level, which is the first one: 45-64. So 5.22 is 65-74 versus 45-64."></div>
</div>

<section class="panel">

<h2>Part 6. How papers present these numbers</h2>

Results text usually gives the odds ratio, its 95% confidence interval, and a p value in one sentence. For the two models you just fit, a paper might say:

<div class="paper-quote">
"Each additional year of age was associated with 12% higher odds of weak grip (OR 1.12, 95% CI 1.11&ndash;1.13, p &lt; 0.001)."
</div>

<div class="paper-quote">
"Compared with men aged 45&ndash;64, men aged 65&ndash;74 had 5.22 times the odds of weak grip (95% CI 4.35&ndash;6.28), while men aged 75+ had 14.44 times the odds (95% CI 11.44&ndash;18.22)."
</div>

Tables follow the same pattern: one column of odds ratios with confidence intervals. Here is a typical table (the smoking row is invented for practice):

<table class="or-table">
  <caption>Table 2. Factors associated with weak grip (illustrative)</caption>
  <thead>
    <tr><th>Predictor</th><th>OR (95% CI)</th></tr>
  </thead>
  <tbody>
    <tr><td>Age, per year</td><td><code>1.12 (1.11&ndash;1.13)</code></td></tr>
    <tr class="refrow"><td>Age group 45&ndash;64</td><td>1 (reference)</td></tr>
    <tr><td>Age group 65&ndash;74</td><td><code>5.22 (4.35&ndash;6.28)</code></td></tr>
    <tr><td>Age group 75+</td><td><code>14.44 (11.44&ndash;18.22)</code></td></tr>
    <tr><td>Current smoking</td><td><code>1.35 (0.98&ndash;1.86)</code></td></tr>
  </tbody>
</table>

</section>

<div class="practice" data-answer="a">
  <div class="practice-title">Question 8</div>
  <p>In the first sentence, where does the <strong>12%</strong> come from?</p>
  <div class="choice-set">
<label><input type="radio" name="p7" value="a">From the odds ratio: 1.12 is 12% above 1.</label>
<label><input type="radio" name="p7" value="b">From the p value.</label>
<label><input type="radio" name="p7" value="c">From the confidence interval width: 1.13 minus 1.11.</label>
  </div>
  <button type="button">Check</button>
  <div class="practice-feedback" data-correct="Correct. The percent wording restates the OR itself: 1.12 - 1 = 0.12, so 12% higher odds per year." data-incorrect="Not quite. The 12% is the OR restated in words: 1.12 is 12% above 1. The CI and p value describe uncertainty, not the size of the effect."></div>
</div>

<div class="callout">
<p><strong>Reading the confidence interval.</strong> The 95% CI gives the range of odds ratios compatible with the data. The value <strong>1</strong> means "no difference", so check whether the interval includes 1. The age CI (1.11 to 1.13) sits entirely above 1: the data clearly point to higher odds. An interval that includes 1 means the data are also compatible with no difference.</p>
</div>

<div class="practice" data-answer="c">
  <div class="practice-title">Question 9</div>
  <p>In the table, current smoking has OR <strong>1.35 (95% CI 0.98&ndash;1.86)</strong>. What is the best reading?</p>
  <div class="choice-set">
<label><input type="radio" name="p8" value="a">Smoking definitely raises the odds of weak grip by 35%.</label>
<label><input type="radio" name="p8" value="b">Smoking lowers the odds of weak grip.</label>
<label><input type="radio" name="p8" value="c">The estimate points to 35% higher odds, but the CI includes 1, so the data are also compatible with no difference.</label>
  </div>
  <button type="button">Check</button>
  <div class="practice-feedback" data-correct="Correct. The best estimate is 35% higher odds, but the interval runs from 0.98 (slightly lower odds) to 1.86, so no difference cannot be ruled out." data-incorrect="Not quite. The estimate (1.35) points to higher odds, but the interval includes 1, so the data are also compatible with no difference. Neither certainty nor a lower-odds claim fits."></div>
</div>

<section class="panel">

<h2>Summary</h2>

<ul class="tight-list">
  <li><strong>Odds</strong> = happens &divide; does not happen = <code>p / (1 - p)</code>.</li>
  <li><strong>Log-odds</strong> = <code>log(odds)</code>. The model's straight line lives on this scale; <code>tidy(mod)</code> reports it.</li>
  <li><strong>Odds ratio</strong> = <code>exp(coefficient)</code>. Get it with <code>tidy(mod, exponentiate = TRUE, conf.int = TRUE)</code>.</li>
  <li>Report the OR in words (percent higher or lower odds, or times the odds), with its 95% CI and p value.</li>
  <li>For categorical predictors, every OR compares one level with the reference level.</li>
</ul>

</section>

<section class="panel completion">

<h2>Completion code</h2>

<p>Answer at least 8 out of 9 questions correctly to reveal your completion code.</p>

<p><span class="code-progress" id="code-progress">0 of 9 correct (need at least 8)</span></p>

<div class="code-box" id="code-box">
  <div class="code-label">Your completion code</div>
  <div class="code-value" id="code-value"></div>
</div>

</section>

<p class="footer-note">GRAPH Courses practical | Odds, log-odds, and odds ratios</p>

</div>

<script>
const COMPLETION_CODE = "EXPODDS";
const COMPLETION_REQUIRED = 8;

function updateCompletion() {
  const cards = document.querySelectorAll(".practice");
  const correct = document.querySelectorAll(".practice.is-correct").length;
  const total = cards.length;
  const progress = document.getElementById("code-progress");
  const box = document.getElementById("code-box");
  const value = document.getElementById("code-value");

  if (progress) {
    progress.textContent = correct + " of " + total + " correct (need at least " + COMPLETION_REQUIRED + ")";
  }

  if (box && value) {
    if (correct >= COMPLETION_REQUIRED) {
      value.textContent = COMPLETION_CODE;
      box.style.display = "block";
    } else {
      box.style.display = "none";
    }
  }
}

document.querySelectorAll(".practice").forEach((card) => {
  const button = card.querySelector("button");
  const feedback = card.querySelector(".practice-feedback");
  const answer = card.dataset.answer;

  button.addEventListener("click", () => {
    const selected = card.querySelector("input[type='radio']:checked");
    card.classList.remove("is-correct", "is-incorrect");
    card.querySelectorAll("label").forEach((label) => {
      label.classList.remove("correct-choice", "incorrect-choice");
    });

    if (!selected) {
      card.classList.add("is-incorrect");
      feedback.textContent = "Choose an answer first, then check it.";
      updateCompletion();
      return;
    }

    const selectedLabel = selected.closest("label");
    const correctInput = card.querySelector(`input[value="${answer}"]`);
    const correctLabel = correctInput ? correctInput.closest("label") : null;

    if (selected.value === answer) {
      card.classList.add("is-correct");
      selectedLabel.classList.add("correct-choice");
      feedback.textContent = feedback.dataset.correct;
    } else {
      card.classList.add("is-incorrect");
      selectedLabel.classList.add("incorrect-choice");
      if (correctLabel) correctLabel.classList.add("correct-choice");
      feedback.textContent = feedback.dataset.incorrect;
    }

    updateCompletion();
  });
});

updateCompletion();
</script>
